segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore you have no excuse, whoever you are, you who judge; for in judging the other person you condemn yourself, because you who judge practice the very same things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we know that the judgment of God falls, in accordance with truth, on those who practice such things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do you suppose, whoever you are, you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you toward turning back?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But in keeping with your hardness and your heart that will not turn back, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who will repay each person according to their works:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but for those who act from selfish ambition and disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: affliction and distress, upon every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there is no favoritism with God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all who sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who sinned under the law will be judged by the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God; rather, the doers of the law will be justified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whenever Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They show the work of the law written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness and their thoughts, one against another, accuse or even defend them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: on the day when God judges the hidden things of people, according to my good news, through Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and know his will and discern what matters, being instructed from the law,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and are confident that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: a corrector of the foolish, a teacher of the immature, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: you, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For, just as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Circumcision is indeed of benefit if you practice the law; but if you are a lawbreaker, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if the uncircumcised man keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the man who is uncircumcised by nature but carries out the law will judge you, who, with the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Jew is not the one who is so in plain view, nor is circumcision what is in plain view, in the flesh;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: rather, the Jew is the one who is so in what is hidden, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not the written code. Such a person's praise comes not from people but from God.

notes.note: The Greek is literally ‘O human being’, a stock form of address to an imagined listener in the ancient debating style known as diatribe. It names no one in particular and is not specific to men, which ‘whoever you are’ conveys. Many scholars think the listener is already the Jewish critic of Gentile vice addressed by name in verse 17; others take it as any moralist at all.

‘Repentance’ now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to ‘return’ to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct; ‘will not turn back’ in verse 5 is the negative of the same word. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term understood to include a change of life.

notes.phrase: who will repay each person according to their works
notes.note: The wording echoes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, and readers who knew the Scriptures would have recognised it. How this judgment according to works fits with Paul's later argument about being justified apart from works of the law is a long-standing debate; the text here states it without qualification.

The adjective is formed from the word for ‘age’. In Jewish usage ‘eternal life’ is the life of the age to come, so the phrase speaks of a kind of life as well as its unending length. ‘Eternal’ is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer ‘life of the age to come’.

The word is rare before the New Testament, where it is used of self-interested pursuit of office. Older translations linked it with a similar-sounding word for strife and rendered ‘contentious’; most lexicons now prefer ‘selfish ambition’ or ‘self-seeking’, though the matter is not settled.

‘Righteous’ and ‘justified’ in this verse, ‘just judgment’ in verse 5, ‘unrighteousness’ in verse 8 and ‘righteous requirements’ in verse 26 all belong to one Greek word-family, which English splits between ‘right’ words and ‘just’ words. ‘Justified’ here means declared to be in the right at God's judgment. Some scholars prefer ‘justice’ language throughout, as translations into most other languages do.

The Greek word means ‘peoples’ or ‘nations’, and in the plural, in Jewish usage, the non-Jewish peoples. English uses ‘Gentiles’ or ‘nations’ according to sense, but it is one word in Greek, here and in the quotation in verse 24.

The phrase can be attached to what follows, as here (they do by nature what the law requires), or to what precedes: Gentiles ‘who do not have the law by nature’, that is, by birth. The first is the majority reading and usually takes these to be Gentiles in general acting on a moral sense. The second is favoured by those who think Paul means Gentile believers, in whom the law is written on the heart as Jeremiah 31:33 promises.

‘Gospel’ has become a religious term and a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between ‘gospel’ and ‘good news’.

The verb's ordinary meaning is to plunder temples, and here it most naturally refers to profiting from the property of pagan shrines, perhaps by trading in goods taken from them, despite professing to abhor idols. Some take it more broadly as ‘commit sacrilege’, including withholding what is owed to the Jerusalem temple. What actual practice Paul has in mind is uncertain.

notes.phrase: blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you
notes.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 52:5 in its ancient Greek version, which includes the words ‘because of you’ and ‘among the Gentiles’; the Hebrew text is shorter. In Isaiah the nations mock God's name because of Israel's exile; Paul applies the line to dishonour brought on God by lawbreaking.

notes.phrase: by the Spirit, not the written code
notes.traditional: in the spirit, not in the letter
notes.note: The Greek has simply ‘in spirit, not letter’. It can mean an inward, spiritual circumcision as against a literal one, or circumcision carried out by God's Spirit as against the written law; Paul's similar contrasts in Romans 7:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:6 favour the second, and most recent commentators adopt it. ‘Letter’ means the law as a written text, as in verse 27, not the modern contrast between the letter and the spirit of a rule.

In Hebrew the name Judah, from which ‘Jew’ derives, is linked with the verb ‘to praise’ (Genesis 29:35; 49:8). Many scholars see a play on that link here: the one who truly bears the name receives praise from God. The pun does not work in Greek, so how many of Paul's first readers would have caught it is uncertain.

candidates.reason: Paul uses it with and without the article throughout Romans and Galatians, and translators differ on ‘law’, ‘the law’ and ‘Law’ in ways readers will notice across chapters.
It is the negative of the δικαιοσύνη family; ‘unrighteousness’, ‘injustice’ and ‘wrongdoing’ are all defensible, and the choice should match the register's handling of that family.
It recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, where it is variously rendered ‘tribulation’, ‘affliction’, ‘trouble’, ‘distress’ or ‘suffering’.
It is frequent in Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation, and translations vary between ‘endurance’, ‘perseverance’, ‘patience’ and ‘steadfastness’.
The letter/Spirit contrast recurs in Romans 7:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, where the traditional ‘letter’ invites the modern ‘letter versus spirit of the law’ misreading.

patch.reason: euangelion promoted to active after full-run drift (good news 37 / gospel 35)
